title: The vow and the fruit out of season
hookLine: a mother gives her unborn child to Allah, and an old guardian finds fruit that shouldn't be there
last: FORGIVE ONE OLD THING, OUT LOUD.

cards: A woman is expecting a child, and she makes a promise before the baby is even born. She tells Allah: whatever is in my womb, I give it to You, set apart for Your service.
In her world, that meant a son, raised to serve in the house of worship. Then the baby comes, and it's a girl. You can almost hear her surprise in the Qur'an.
My Lord, I've given birth to a girl, she says, and the Qur'an adds that Allah knew best what she had delivered. She keeps the vow anyway.
She names her daughter Maryam, and asks Allah to protect her and her children from Shaytan. This is how the Qur'an begins the story of Maryam: with her mother.

teach.h: THE WIFE OF 'IMRAN KEEPS HER VOW.
teach.b: The Qur'an calls her mother simply the wife of 'Imran. It doesn't give her a name; later tradition calls her Hannah. The whole family gives its name to a surah: Al 'Imran, the family of 'Imran, the third chapter.
Allah accepts the girl with a beautiful acceptance, the verse says, and makes her grow up well. An old man named Zakariyya becomes her guardian.

teach.h: A MIHRAB: THE ROOM OF PRAYER.
teach.b: Maryam lives and prays in a small room in the place of worship, a mihrab. The same word now names the niche in a mosque's wall that shows which way to pray.
And every time Zakariyya goes in to see her, he finds food there. Food he didn't bring.
So he asks her, in Pickthall's old English: “O Mary! Whence cometh unto thee this (food)?” And the girl answers, simply: “It is from Allah. Allah giveth without stint to whom He will.”

In Arabic, bi-ghayri hisab: without counting, without reckoning. Early commentators said Zakariyya found summer fruit in winter, and winter fruit in summer. The verse itself only says food, so that detail is theirs.
Now notice who teaches whom. The old guardian, a man of prayer, asks the question. The girl gives the answer.
Commentators point out that Maryam is the only woman the Qur'an calls by her own name.

teach.h: NAMED, WITH A SURAH OF HER OWN.
teach.b: A whole surah, the nineteenth, is named for her.
Muslims honor her as one of the best women who ever lived.

how: Muslims read the story of Maryam's birth in Surah Al 'Imran and honor her as one of the best of women; some use her answer, 'it is from Allah', as a way of receiving unexpected good.

only after a long and careful reckoning

games.q: you're Zakariyya. every time you visit the girl in your care, there's food in her room that nobody brought. what do you do?
o: ask her where it comes from.
search the room for a hidden visitor.
say nothing and take the food away.
games.why: he asks, whence cometh unto thee this? and the girl answers: it is from Allah. Allah giveth without stint to whom He will (3:37).

practice: Go back over the last week for something you didn't plan and didn't earn, a text from an old friend, a parking spot, a stranger's kindness, a song at the right moment, something simply there when you walked in, like fruit in Maryam's room, and hold it for a moment.
If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah for it; if not, just let yourself be surprised by it again.

wordCard.voice: Bi-ghayri hisab, without measure: how Maryam said her food came, when Zakariyya found what no one had brought.
